title: Calibrate a drone's compass: turn it a full turn held level, then a full turn held vertically, passing it hand to hand
instruction: Calibrate the drone's compass: pick it up, hold it level and turn it one full turn, then hold it vertically, nose down or nose up, and turn it one full turn. Do not put it down in between. Then stand it back on its pad.
context: A drone's compass is calibrated by hand before it flies somewhere new. The maker's manual says to hold the aircraft horizontally and rotate it 360 degrees, then hold it vertically and rotate it 360 degrees about a vertical axis; it recommends this after travelling more than 50 km, after 30 days unused, or when the app warns of interference. The United States has 837,513 registered drones and 481,760 certificated remote pilots (the aviation regulator's count, November 2025). For a robot it is a test of regrasping a free object. A wrist turns about two thirds of a circle, so a full turn of something held in the air needs it passed from one hand to the other and back without being put down, and going from level to vertical needs a different grasp. Nothing fixes the drone: whichever hand has it carries its whole weight, and the grasps have to avoid its propellers, arms, legs and camera.
setup: Cm from the midpoint between the arm bases, x away from the robot, y left; heights above the table; directions in degrees from straight away from the robot, anticlockwise seen from above. Landing pad: a square orange rubber mat, 24 x 24 x 0.4, fixed, centred at (26, -7). Drone: a folding camera drone of 249 g, unfolded, propellers on, standing on its four legs with its middle over the pad's centre, nose pointing 270 degrees (toward the robot's right). Fuselage 13.8 long (camera block at the nose included) x 5.8 wide x 4 tall, grey plastic, its underside 0.75 above the pad. Four arms 1.3 wide leave it 6.25 ahead of and behind its middle; each carries a motor 8.95 out to the side, a two-blade 11 cm propeller with its blades pointing out sideways (28.9 across the propellers) and a leg. 5.6 tall from feet to propellers. Both arms start in their ready pose. Layout B (DRONE_LOT=B): the pad at (23.5, -10), the nose pointing 180 degrees (toward the robot).
scoring: A turn counts over one unbroken hold: from when the drone's lowest point rises 2 cm above the table until it comes back within 2 cm. Level turn: done when the nose has pointed in all 36 ten-degree compass directions while the drone's top was within 20 degrees of straight up. Upright turn: done when, after the level turn and in the same hold, its top has faced all 36 directions while its nose-to-tail line was within 20 degrees of plumb. A drop: coming within 2 cm of the table faster than 0.25 m/s. At the end the drone stands if its top is within 10 degrees of up, its lowest point is within 3 mm of the pad's top or the table, and it is at rest (under 2 cm/s and 0.5 rad/s). 0.25: level turn done. 0.5: both turns done. 0.75: both done, never dropped, standing at the end. 1.0: also all four feet over the pad and both grippers at least 3 cm from the drone. 0 otherwise.
reset_notes: Stand the drone back on its pad with its nose on the start mark. After a drop, check the propellers, the legs and the camera before the next trial.
fidelity: One rigid body of boxes at full size. Sourced (the maker's manual): 249 g; 138 mm long folded; unfolded 289 mm across the propellers, 56 mm tall. Estimates: the fuselage's 58 x 40 mm section, where the arms, motors and legs are, the 110 mm propellers, friction, the 20-degree limits (the manual gives none). Simplified: propellers fixed with blades out sideways (real ones turn and fold); no status light or compass, the score is from the measured motion. Pad fixed. Not tried on a physical rig.
scores: Dream-1 run: 0.0 (the right arm went to the drone several times and drew back; the left arm stayed folded by its base; the drone was not lifted and ended on its pad where it started); demo: 1.0 (the trial ended with full score at step 2,077 of 3,000)
